{{short description|Twisting of an object due to an applied torque}}
{{Redirect|Torsional|other notions of torsion|Torsion (disambiguation)}}
[[File:Twisted bar.png|thumb|right|Torsion of a square-section bar]]
[[File:Torsion Blender.gif|thumb|Example of torsion mechanics]]

In [[solid mechanics]], '''torsion''' is the twisting of an object caused by an applied [[torque]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Escudier |first=Marcel |title=A Dictionary of Mechanical Engineering |date=2019 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-883210-2 |location=New York, NY}}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia |doi=10.1093/acref/9780198821472.001.0001 |encyclopedia=A Dictionary of Physics |date=2019 |isbn=978-0-19-882147-2 |editor-last1=Rennie |editor-first1=Richard |editor-last2=Law |editor-first2=Jonathan |title=torsion |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780198821472.001.0001/acref-9780198821472-e-3112 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> It may be described as an angular deformation,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lindsay |first=Robert Bruce |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001478181 |title=Student's Handbook of Elementary Physics |date=1943 |publisher=The Dryden Press |location=New York, NY}}</ref> measured by the rotation of a cross-section from its undeformed position.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Michels |first=Walter C. |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/001477465 |title=The International Dictionary of Physics and Electronics |date=1956 |publisher=Van Nostrand |location=Princeton, NJ}}</ref> Torque is commonly expressed in [[newton metre]]s (N·m) or [[foot-pound force]] (ft·lbf), while the resulting torsional [[shear stress]] is expressed in [[Pascal (unit)|pascals]] (Pa) or [[pounds per square inch]] (psi).

In a circular shaft, the shear stress is tangent to circles centred on the shaft axis. In non-circular cross-sections, twisting is accompanied by [[warping]], so transverse sections do not generally remain plane.<ref>{{cite book |title=Torsional Analysis of Structural Steel Members |publisher=[[American Institute of Steel Construction]] |last1=Seaburg |first1=Paul |last2=Carter |first2=Charles |year=1997 |page=3}}</ref> Under uniform, unrestrained [[Saint-Venant torsion]], torque and twist are related by

:<math>T=GJ_\mathrm{T}\Theta=\frac{GJ_\mathrm{T}}{\ell}\varphi,</math>

where <math>T</math> is the torque, <math>G</math> is the [[shear modulus]], <math>J_\mathrm{T}</math> is the Saint-Venant [[torsion constant]], <math>\Theta=\mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}x</math> is the twist rate, <math>\varphi</math> is the total angle of twist over the length <math>\ell</math>, and <math>GJ_\mathrm{T}</math> is the torsional rigidity. The geometric quantity <math>J_\mathrm{T}</math> has dimensions of length to the fourth power. Only for circular shafts is the stress distribution simply

:<math>\tau(r)=\frac{Tr}{J_\mathrm{T}}.</math>

Closed-form solutions are available for only a limited number of cross-sections. Thin open sections are commonly approximated by a sum of rectangular strips, while thin closed cells are commonly treated with Bredt's formula. More general sections are usually analysed numerically or by variational bounds.<ref name="TimoshenkoGoodier1970">{{cite book |last1=Timoshenko |first1=Stephen P. |last2=Goodier |first2=James N. |title=Theory of Elasticity |edition=3rd |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1970}}</ref> In 2026, Rocco Ditommaso and Felice Carlo Ponzo presented an [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020722526001813 open-access] exact-arithmetic primal–dual procedure that provides certified lower and upper bounds for solid, open and hollow polygonal sections.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026">{{cite journal
 |last1=Ditommaso
 |first1=Rocco
 |last2=Ponzo
 |first2=Felice Carlo
 |year=2026
 |title=Certified Saint-Venant torsional stiffness of solid, open and hollow polygonal sections: An exact-arithmetic primal–dual method based on closed-form analytical formulae for engineering section analysis
 |journal=International Journal of Engineering Science
 |volume=228
 |article-number=104643
 |doi=10.1016/j.ijengsci.2026.104643
 |doi-access=free
|hdl=11563/218178
 |hdl-access=free
 }}</ref>

== Properties ==

For a circular shaft, the shear stress at radius <math>r</math> is

:<math>\tau(r)=\frac{Tr}{J_\mathrm{T}}.</math>

The maximum shear stress therefore occurs at the outer surface. Surface stress concentrations caused by notches, roughness or abrupt geometric changes can further increase the local stress.

For a prismatic member of constant cross-section and constant torque, the angle of twist is

:<math>\varphi=\frac{T\ell}{GJ_\mathrm{T}}.</math>

For non-circular sections, <math>J_\mathrm{T}</math> is generally not equal to the polar second moment of area, and the shear-stress distribution is not proportional to the distance from the axis.

== Torsion constants for common cross-sections ==

The following tables distinguish exact solutions, engineering asymptotic formulas and certified bounds. The symbol <math>J_\mathrm{T}</math> denotes the geometric torsion constant; the physical torsional rigidity is <math>GJ_\mathrm{T}</math>.

=== Exact and engineering formulas ===

{| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; font-size:90%;"
! style="width:20%;" | Cross-section
! style="width:31%;" | Torsion constant
! Stress or validity
|-
| Solid circle, radius <math>R</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}=\frac{\pi R^4}{2}</math>
| Exact. <math>\displaystyle \tau_{\max}=\frac{2T}{\pi R^3}</math> at <math>r=R</math>.<ref name="TimoshenkoGoodier1970" />
|-
| Ellipse, semi-axes <math>p\geq q</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}=\frac{\pi p^3q^3}{p^2+q^2}</math>
| Exact. <math>\displaystyle \tau_{\max}=\frac{2T}{\pi p q^2}</math>, attained at the ends of the minor axis.<ref name="TimoshenkoGoodier1970" />
|-
| Circular annulus, radii <math>R_i<R_e</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(R_e^4-R_i^4\right)</math>
| Exact. <math>\displaystyle \tau_{\max}=\frac{2TR_e}{\pi\left(R_e^4-R_i^4\right)}</math>.<ref name="TimoshenkoGoodier1970" />
|-
| Equilateral triangle, side <math>a</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{80}a^4</math>
| Exact. It is the only triangular section for which a cubic Prandtl stress function proportional to <math>\lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3</math> is an exact solution.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Compact rectangle, sides <math>b\geq t</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}=\alpha(b/t)\,b t^3</math>
| The coefficient <math>\alpha</math> is obtained from a Fourier-series solution or tabulated values; there is no elementary closed form.<ref name="TimoshenkoGoodier1970" />
|-
| Thin rectangle, length <math>a</math>, thickness <math>s</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\simeq\frac{1}{3}as^3</math>
| Thin-strip approximation, valid for <math>a/s\gg1</math>. <math>\displaystyle \tau_{\max}\simeq\frac{3T}{as^2}</math>.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Open section made of thin rectangular walls
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\simeq\frac{1}{3}\sum_i b_i t_i^3</math>
| Engineering thin-strip sum; valid when the individual walls are slender and junction effects are negligible.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Thin closed single-cell section
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\simeq\frac{4A_m^2}{\displaystyle\oint\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{t(s)}}</math>
| Bredt approximation. <math>A_m</math> is the area enclosed by the wall mid-line and <math>t(s)</math> is the local thickness. The shear stress is <math>\displaystyle \tau(s)\simeq\frac{T}{2A_m t(s)}</math>.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|}

== Certified primal–dual method ==

In 2026, [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0020722526001813 Rocco Ditommaso and Felice Carlo Ponzo] proposed an exact-arithmetic primal–dual procedure for certifying the Saint-Venant torsion constant of polygonal sections.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" /> For a convex polygon with rational vertex coordinates, the boundary function <math>B_0=\prod_i\ell_i</math> is multiplied by a polynomial <math>q_p</math> to form a kinematically admissible field <math>v_p=B_0q_p</math>. A statically admissible field is constructed as <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma}_p=(-x,-y)+\nabla^\perp\psi_p</math>. Optimising the two fields gives a lower and an upper bound,

:<math>J_p^-=4\mathbf{g}^{\mathsf T}K^{-1}\mathbf{g}\leq J_\mathrm{T}\leq J_p^+=\int_\Omega(x^2+y^2)\,\mathrm{d}A-\mathbf{b}^{\mathsf T}M_{\mathrm{red}}^{-1}\mathbf{b}.</math>

Because the required integrals reduce to polynomial moments over rational triangles, the endpoints and the interval width are exact rational numbers rather than floating-point estimates. The width is the energy mismatch

:<math>J_p^+-J_p^-=\int_\Omega\left|\boldsymbol{\sigma}_p-\nabla v_p\right|^2\,\mathrm{d}A.</math>

The same construction extends to non-convex open sections by using piecewise polynomial spaces on rational triangulations, and to multiply connected hollow sections by adding constants and flux constraints on the internal boundaries. The method does not replace the classical exact or thin-wall formulas; instead, it brackets the true value when no elementary formula exists and quantifies the error and sign of engineering approximations.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />

=== Examples of certified relations ===

{| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; font-size:90%;"
! style="width:22%;" | Section or class
! style="width:43%;" | Certified relation
! Notes
|-
| Convex rational polygon
| <math>\displaystyle J_p^-\leq J_\mathrm{T}\leq J_p^+</math>
| Global polynomial primal–dual certificate. Both endpoints are exact rational numbers.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Scalene triangle, area <math>A</math>, side lengths <math>a_1,a_2,a_3</math>
| <math>\displaystyle \frac{4A^3}{5\left(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2\right)}\leq J_\mathrm{T}</math>
<br />
<math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\leq\frac{A}{36}\left(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2\right)</math>
| Elementary two-sided certified interval.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Compact rectangle, sides <math>b\geq t</math>
| <math>\displaystyle \frac{5b^3t^3}{18\left(b^2+t^2\right)}\leq J_\mathrm{T}</math>
<br />
<math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\leq\frac{bt\left(b^2+t^2\right)}{12}</math>
| Elementary bounds. Tighter degree-dependent rational bounds are given in Appendix C of the open-access article.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Isosceles trapezoid, bases <math>b_1,b_2</math>, height <math>h</math>
| <math>\displaystyle J_0^-(b_1,b_2,h)\leq J_\mathrm{T}\leq J_0^+(b_1,b_2,h)</math>
| Closed parametric expressions are given in equations (C.4) and (C.5) of the open-access article; they are omitted here because of their length.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Open section decomposed into disjoint rectangular walls
| <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\geq\sum_i\frac{5b_i^3t_i^3}{18\left(b_i^2+t_i^2\right)}</math>
| Certified lower bound, in contrast with the asymptotic thin-strip sum.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Non-convex open or hollow polygon
| <math>\displaystyle J_h^-\leq J_\mathrm{T}\leq J_h^+</math>
| Piecewise polynomial certificate on a rational triangulation. Hollow sections also require internal-boundary constants and flux constraints.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|-
| Sharp-corner rectangular tube, external dimensions <math>b\times h</math>, thickness <math>t</math>
| Let <math>A_m=(b-t)(h-t)</math>, <math>b_i=b-2t</math>, and <math>h_i=h-2t</math>.
<br />
<math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{ramp}^-=
\frac{2t\left(A_m+t^2/3\right)^2}{b+h-2t}
\leq J_\mathrm{T}</math>
<br />
<math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{T}\leq J_0^+=
\frac{bh\left(b^2+h^2\right)-b_i h_i\left(b_i^2+h_i^2\right)}{12}</math>
| The Bredt value is <math>\displaystyle J_\mathrm{Bredt}=\frac{2tA_m^2}{b+h-2t}</math>, and <math>J_\mathrm{Bredt}\leq J_\mathrm{ramp}^-</math> for the stated family.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|}

=== Reliability of commonly used relations ===

{| class="wikitable" style="width:100%; font-size:90%;"
! Type
! Examples
! Interpretation
|-
| Exact closed form
| Circle, ellipse, circular annulus, equilateral triangle
| Gives the exact Saint-Venant torsion constant.
|-
| Engineering or asymptotic formula
| Thin-strip sum for open sections; Bredt formula for closed cells
| Useful under geometric assumptions, but not a guaranteed bound in general.
|-
| Certified interval
| Exact-arithmetic primal–dual bounds for rational polygonal sections
| Guarantees <math>J^-\leq J_\mathrm{T}\leq J^+</math>; the interval width measures the residual uncertainty.<ref name="DitommasoPonzo2026" />
|}

== Sample calculation ==

[[File:Dampfturbine Laeufer01.jpg|thumb|250px|The rotor of a modern [[steam turbine]]]]

Consider a solid circular shaft transmitting 1000 [[megawatt]]s at a rotational frequency of 50 [[hertz]]. Let the allowable shear stress initially be 250&nbsp;MPa.

The [[angular frequency]] is

:<math>\omega=2\pi f,</math>

and the transmitted torque is

:<math>T=\frac{P}{\omega}.</math>

For <math>P=1.0\times10^9</math>&nbsp;W and <math>f=50</math>&nbsp;Hz, <math>\omega=314.16</math>&nbsp;rad/s and <math>T\approx3.1831\times10^6</math>&nbsp;N·m.

For a solid circular shaft,

:<math>J_\mathrm{T}=\frac{\pi D^4}{32}</math>

and

:<math>\tau_{\max}=\frac{16T}{\pi D^3}.</math>

Solving for the diameter gives

:<math>D=\left(\frac{16T}{\pi\tau_{\max}}\right)^{1/3}.</math>

The resulting diameter is approximately 0.40&nbsp;m. With a [[factor of safety]] of 5, so that the allowable stress is 50&nbsp;MPa, the diameter increases to approximately 0.69&nbsp;m.

== Failure modes ==

The shear stress in a shaft under pure torsion may be resolved into [[principal stress]]es using [[Mohr's circle]]. The principal tensile and compressive stresses act on planes oriented at approximately 45° to the shaft axis. Brittle materials may therefore fail along a helical fracture surface inclined at about 45°, as can be demonstrated by twisting a piece of chalk.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Fakouri Hasanabadi
 |first1=M.
 |last2=Kokabi
 |first2=A. H.
 |last3=Faghihi-Sani
 |first3=M. A.
 |last4=Groß-Barsnick
 |first4=S. M.
 |last5=Malzbender
 |first5=J.
 |title=Room- and high-temperature torsional shear strength of solid oxide fuel/electrolysis cell sealing material
 |journal=Ceramics International
 |date=February 2019
 |volume=45
 |issue=2
 |pages=2219–2225
 |doi=10.1016/j.ceramint.2018.10.134
}}</ref>

A ductile circular shaft may instead undergo substantial plastic shear deformation before fracture. Because an axisymmetric shaft can retain its overall external shape while accumulating permanent twist, overload damage may not be visually obvious.<ref>{{cite web
 |last=Clyne
 |first=Bill
 |title=Bending and Torsion of Beams
 |url=https://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/beam_bending/twisting.php
 |website=University of Cambridge Dissemination of IT for the Promotion of Materials Science (DoITPoMS)
 |publisher=University of Cambridge
 |access-date=2 July 2026
}}</ref>

Thin-walled hollow shafts may also fail by torsional buckling, producing diagonal wrinkles typically oriented at approximately 45° to the shaft axis.

== Torsional resonator ==

A torsional resonator uses rotational motion to investigate the elastic or viscoelastic behaviour of a fibre or other slender specimen. A typical system consists of a fibre fixed at one end and connected at the other end to a rigid rod or inertial mass.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Heinisch
 |first1=Martin
 |last2=Niedermayer
 |first2=Alexander O.
 |last3=Dufour
 |first3=Isabelle
 |last4=Jakoby
 |first4=Bernhard
 |title=Concept Studies of Torsional Resonators for Viscosity and Mass Density Sensing Applications
 |journal=Procedia Engineering
 |date=2014
 |volume=87
 |pages=1198–1201
 |doi=10.1016/j.proeng.2014.11.381
 |doi-access=free
}}</ref> The deformation and damping of the fibre provide information about energy dissipation and viscoelasticity.

A simple rotational equation of motion is<ref name="Shull2025">{{cite web
 |last=Shull
 |first=Ken
 |date=5 May 2025
 |title=Mechanical Properties of Materials
 |publisher=Northwestern University
 |url=http://msecore.northwestern.edu/406/406text.pdf
}}</ref>

:<math>T_\mathrm{ext}=K_t\theta+I\frac{\mathrm{d}^2\theta}{\mathrm{d}t^2},</math>

where <math>T_\mathrm{ext}</math> is the applied torque, <math>\theta</math> is the angular displacement, <math>K_t</math> is the torsional spring stiffness and <math>I</math> is the rotational moment of inertia.

For a cylindrical fibre of diameter <math>d</math> and length <math>l</math>,

:<math>K_t=\frac{\pi Gd^4}{32l}.</math>

The undamped natural angular frequency is

:<math>\omega_n=\sqrt{\frac{K_t}{I}}.</math>

For an ideal elastic material undergoing free undamped oscillation,

:<math>\theta=\theta_0\cos(\omega_n t).</math>

Viscoelastic behaviour may be represented by a complex shear modulus

:<math>G^*=G'+iG'',</math>

where <math>G'</math> is the shear [[storage modulus]] and <math>G''</math> is the shear [[loss modulus]]. The corresponding complex stiffness and frequency describe both the elastic response and damping.<ref>{{cite book
 |last1=Meyers
 |first1=Marc A.
 |last2=Chawla
 |first2=Krishan K.
 |title=Mechanical Behavior of Materials
 |date=2009
 |publisher=Cambridge University Press
 |isbn=978-0-511-45557-5
 |edition=2nd
 |location=Cambridge, UK
}}</ref>

Valtorta and Mazza used a torsional resonator device to measure the viscoelastic properties of soft tissue by characterising its complex shear modulus.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Valtorta
 |first1=Davide
 |last2=Mazza
 |first2=Edoardo
 |title=Dynamic measurement of soft tissue viscoelastic properties with a torsional resonator device
 |journal=Medical Image Analysis
 |date=October 2005
 |volume=9
 |issue=5
 |pages=481–490
 |doi=10.1016/j.media.2005.05.002
 |pmid=16006169
}}</ref>
